https://www.politico.eu/article/us-will-.text: DUBLIN — Closer ties between the EU and Canada won't mean a worse relationship between the bloc and the U.S., according to Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris. In an interview the day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pitched making Ottawa an "associate member" of the EU, Harris said that closer ties with Canada "is not about having a less close relationship with anybody." "Ultimately the U.S. administration will understand that because it's the truth,” Harris, also Ireland's deputy finance minister, added. Advertisement Advertisement Von der Leyen's suggestion, as part of her Wednesday "State of the Union" speech, has not gone down well in Washington, D.C., however. U.S. President Donald Trump warned it could be viewed as a “hostile act” which could see him hitting the bloc with “ very heavy tariffs .” Harris played down the reaction. “The European Union and the U.S., politics aside, have an extraordinarily interdependent economic trading relationship,” he said. “We always judge the U.S. administration based on what they do, rather than initial comments, but the reality is we have a very close relationship with the United States economically.” Asked whether the EU will need to choose which trading relationship to prioritize between the U.S. and Canada in future, Harris said: “I certainly hope not.” Canada's in town The dramatic announcements around Canada and the EU's future relationship have come amid a flurry of economic diplomacy between the two sides. Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will join a gathering of EU finance ministers hosted by Harris in Dublin Friday, after Prime Minister Mark Carney’s whistle-stop tour this week. Advertisement Advertisement The finance ministers of the U.K., Ukraine and Switzerland are also joining to give updates on their economies and hold one-to-one meetings, despite the summit being consumed by disagreements over the EU's next seven-year budget. Meanwhile, the head of the European Investment Bank, Nadia Calviño, will head to Ottawa on Sunday to lay the groundwork for Europe-Canada cooperation on critical raw materials. Harris said: “It's a real vote of confidence in the European Union, quite frankly, that a country and an economy as big as Canada wants to cooperate.” “Some countries are choosing to look inwards, that's their right. The European Union wants to continue to be outward-looking. It's a positive development, it's not a development against anybody,” he added. Von der Leyen’s pitch to make Canada an associate member — a legal status that currently doesn’t exist — has ruffled feathers among EU capitals after she made the surprise announcement in a major speech on Wednesday. Carney has said he welcomes the plan's ambition, but stopped short of a full endorsement . Harris was positive on the pitch, calling it “really exciting” and pointing to climate and cybersecurity as two issues where the EU and Canada could cooperate. Advertisement Advertisement “I'm less concerned about what you call it, and more enthused by the idea that Canada and the European Union want to work together on a program of substance,” he said. Trump visited Ireland last weekend, lifting the 10% U.S. tariff charge on Irish whiskey products as a gesture of goodwill. “We definitely don’t want to have that [whiskey tariff] back,” Harris said.

https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: Italy on Tuesday extended border checks on visitors from Spain for another 15 days, checks it first imposed after more than 72,000 migrants poured into Spain's North African territory of Ceuta from Morocco in late July, AP reported.Spain, which had responded to Rome's measures with its own retaliatory border checks on travellers from Italy, also extended its tit-for-tat controls for another 15 days, the Spanish foreign ministry said.How the crisis beganThe standoff traces back to July 30-31, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta from Morocco in one of the largest single border surges the enclave has ever seen, according to the UK House of Commons Library.Also read: Morocco, 60,000 migrants and Spain’s Ceuta crisis: All we know so farItalian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government responded on July 31 by suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain, saying the move was needed to protect the security of our citizens and defend Europe's borders, and describing the uncontrolled immigration in Ceuta as a threat to Italy's national security.The move triggered a wider European reaction. Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called for the EU to consider all options, including a suspension of Schengen cooperation with Spain, while Finland's Interior Minister Mari Rantanen backed Italy's approach and said Helsinki was weighing similar measures.The Czech Republic's Andrej Babiš went further, calling for Spain's Schengen membership itself to be temporarily suspended, while France and Portugal moved to tighten their own border security.Spain hit back roughly a week later, imposing its own passport and identity checks on travellers from Italy starting August 8, after issuing Rome a 48-hour ultimatum to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens. Italy refused to back down, with Meloni's government maintaining that its checks were necessary to guard against security risks stemming from the migrant surge.Extending the standoff, againAlthough most of the migrants involved in the July surge were eventually returned to Morocco, Meloni's government and other hawkish European leaders seized on the chaos in Ceuta to criticise the migration policies of Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, whose government had carried out a sweeping migrant legalisation drive just months earlier.Italy's border checks amount to random police screening of passengers arriving from Spain at airports and seaports, justified on the grounds of a threat to internal security. The Italian Interior Ministry invoked the same justification on Tuesday to extend the checks further, saying in a statement that it had informed the European Union and other European governments that high risks to internal security persist, in addition to a potential threat related to possible terrorist infiltration. Spain, for its part, said it was extending its retaliatory measures simply because the conditions that prompted them, Italy's original sanctions, remained unchanged.Visa-free travel, with a catchThe EU's 27-member Schengen area normally allows citizens of most member states to travel across internal borders without passport checks. Under EU rules, member states may temporarily reintroduce such checks in the event of a serious threat, including to internal security, but the rules also stipulate that such controls should be a last resort in exceptional circumstances and must be strictly time-limited.Even before Italy's checks began, travellers leaving Ceuta and Melilla, Spain's other North African territory, were already subject to EU border checks at ports and airports. NGOs have reported that more than 140 people died attempting to cross into Ceuta during the July surge, including people who drowned or were trampled in a stampede to scale a breakwater barrier, a toll that rose sharply from initial estimates of around 34 deaths reported in the crisis's immediate aftermath.A political liability for SanchezMore than 5,000 migrants remain in Ceuta, prolonging a humanitarian crisis that has become a significant political liability for Sanchez both domestically and internationally. His visit to the enclave was met with protests, with residents booing him and chanting for his resignation while declaring Ceuta is not for sale, according to earlier reporting.Also read: Ceuta migrant crisis: Spain breaks silence with firm sovereignty messageThe controversy is closely tied to Sanchez's decision to carry out an amnesty for migrants without residency permits who could prove they had lived in Spain for at least five months and arrived before January 1 this year, a scheme that drew more than 1 million applications before its window closed.The European Commission has said it does not see a direct link between that regularisation programme and the Ceuta crossings, but the political damage from the association has persisted.(With inputs from AP)

Photograph: Cameron Jones-Manley/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Opinion Ukraine Putin’s escalating bombing campaign won’t break Ukrainians’ resolve. History shows that it’s doomed to fail Rajan Menon As winter approaches and the fifth anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion looms, it’s worth remembering that this mode of warfare rarely crushes morale Mon 5 Oct 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 07.08 EDT Share V ladimir Putin’s army hasn’t made much headway in Ukraine this year, and his territorial goals – annexing four Ukrainian provinces – remain elusive, despite more than four and a half years of war. That explains his recent efforts to sap Ukrainians’ will to resist by launching relentless drone and missile strikes against their cities – targeting, among other sites, residential buildings, large open-air markets, shopping malls, the Dobrobut medical centre and the National Academy of Sciences, both in Kyiv. The capital has been hit the hardest, but other cities – Dnipro , Kharkiv, Kherson, Odesa , Mykolaiv, Sumy – haven’t been spared. Air-raid sirens pierce the quiet of night. People scramble to shelters (assuming there are any nearby) or, in Kyiv, race to below-ground subway stations. Even walking along city streets, shopping, or filling up your car at a garage forecourt – which are prime targets – can lead to injury, or even death. I got a taste of what these unremitting attacks are like during a September trip to Ukraine . One night in Mykolaiv, I counted more than a dozen alerts between midnight and dawn. In Kopyliv, about 31 miles west of Kyiv, I was having dinner in a restaurant when a deafening bang made the walls shudder. A drone had hit a building about 500m away; orange flames engulfed its roof within seconds. Incidents like this are now part of daily life for Ukrainians, but are no less nerve-racking for that. During September, Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered drones , mainly Geran variants, at Ukraine: nearly 12% more than in August, and a massive increase compared with 350 such strikes in June. Drones, jet-powered or not, are often supplemented by ballistic missiles such as the Iskander – devilishly difficult to intercept with its top speed of 5,600mph and ability to swerve in flight. The purpose of Putin’s escalating bombardment is to make life so unbearable for Ukrainians that they conclude that the only way out is to satisfy his unfulfilled annexationist ambitions: his army occupies almost all of Luhansk, but has yet to conquer the regions of Donetsk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia completely. Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon Tisdall Read more But his drone and missile campaign won’t force Ukraine to cave. In December 2025, a Kyiv International Institute of Sociology poll revealed that Ukrainians’ resistance to trading land for peace remains strong. Three-quarters of those surveyed rejected a hypothetical deal that included these provisions: Ukraine’s withdrawal from the unoccupied part of Donetsk, recognition of Russia’s legal ownership of Crimea and Donbas, and the abandonment of its Nato aspirations. Asked separately whether they would approve a settlement that required ceding the unoccupied parts of the two southern provinces, two-thirds said no. These responses are all the more significant because by the end of last year, Russia had begun attacking Ukraine’s power grid as a brutal winter approached. Putin might nevertheless calculate that a massive bombing operation this winter that turns off the lights, disrupts heating and damages waterworks and sanitation systems will break Ukrainians’ willpower, creating conditions for Russia to conclude the war with additional territory in hand. His calculation isn’t unreasonable, considering Ukraine’s severe shortage of ballistic missile interceptors, which reduced interceptions from 70% in March to 20% in July. It’s collaborating with a European coalition to develop the cost-effective Freya ballistic missile defence system, and will acquire the Franco-Italian SAMP/T NG missile defence system, which provides far easier mobility to aid rapid relocation and is now under development. Neither, however, will be deployed in sufficient numbers any time soon. Still, the Russian leader’s strategy collides with some inconvenient facts, quite apart from Ukrainians’ proven toughness. The historical record shows that bombing campaigns don’t crush morale; they strengthen it. Ukrainians won’t be the exception. They regard resistance to Russia as essential for national survival. When I’ve asked them why they continue to fight, the reply, in one form or another, is that the alternative is to forfeit their independence. One can dismiss this as bravado, but what matters is that Ukrainians hold this view. Accompanying it is the widespread belief that Putin will use any deal to buy time and regroup before renewing his assault on Ukraine. This, too, makes Ukrainians wary of land-for-peace formulas, particularly those offered by Donald Trump and his two emissaries, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, whom they consider Putin partisans, rather than disinterested mediators. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion Besides, Putin, too, is under pressure. According to the chief of the UK’s defence staff, his army has suffered 1.5 million casualties. And though Ukraine has a military manpower shortage, so does Russia, despite a population that’s 3.5 times larger; hence its reliance on North Korean soldiers and Asian and African mercenaries. Moreover, the Russian army has barely gained any additional territory this year. During the first six months of 2026, it captured only 28% as much land as it did in the same period last year, and its troop losses now exceed its monthly intake by 6,000 . Furthermore, Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia’s roads and rail lines traversing Ukraine’s occupied territory in the south have left its troops in Crimea, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia short of critical supplies. Most recently, Operation Vivaldi , conducted by Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, caught Russian troops by surprise in the Lyman sector of northern Donetsk, forcing them to retreat eastward. The war has harmed Russia’s economy. The army’s huge appetite for manpower has created severe labour shortages that have hurt businesses. The 2027 budget draft allocates 35% of federal expenditures to defence. Ukraine’s strikes on refineries deep inside Russia had cut their throughput by about 30% , year on year, by June, creating chronic fuel shortages, widespread rationing , serpentine lines at petrol stations and a 21% surge in petrol prices since January. Taken together, Ukrainians’ opposition to sacrificing land, the historical failure of bombing campaigns to shatter civilian morale and Russia’s own assorted problems suggest that Putin’s drones and missiles won’t force Ukraine to accept peace on his terms – even under the stress of winter. Rajan Menon is a professor emeritus of international relations at the City College of New York and a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Saltzman Institute of War and Peace Studies Explore more on these topics Ukraine Opinion Russia Vladimir Putin Europe comment Share Reuse this content Comments ( … ) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.wrestlinginc.com/2266023/wwe.text: WWE NXT Star Mason Rook Comments On Grabbing The Attention Of John Cena By Daisy Ruth Sept. 27, 2026 9:30 am EST WWE Add Wrestling Inc. on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover "WWE NXT" star Mason Rook, the former Will Kroos on the UK independent scene, made a big impact when he debuted in WWE , immediately going after then-NXT Champion Tony D'Angelo. Since then, he's won a number one contender's match to challenge Grayson Waller for the gold . One of Rook's most vocal fans is WWE legend John Cena . Cena has recalled first being exposed to Rook , and instantly becoming a fan, when he watched Rook's work while filming a movie in Budapest. Rook spoke on " Busted Open Radio " about what Cena's support means to him. He said it's "very surreal" and explained he first met Cena while doing extra work for WWE in Glasgow. "We were all walking into the extra room and he was in there signing some 8x10s in one of the production rooms," he said. "Obviously, of course I saw him, and we were walking in, and I thought at the time he was getting up to leave... I just thought to myself, 'This may be the only time I ever get to introduce myself and say 'hello' to him.'" Rook said he shook Cena's hand, and Cena told him the story of watching him on an independent wrestling channel in Budapest. The "NXT" star said at first, he thought it was a rib, since he didn't know Cena's personality. Rook said Cena's quick support is a credit to his work, but it has still been incredible for him. "For John not only give his time to me then, but obviously since I've arrived in WWE, he's been quite vocal of myself, too," Rook said. "He's not had to do that, so I'm forever grateful for him for that." https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/20/time.text: US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he wanted his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia as he complained that the United States had received "nothing back" for its support for Kyiv.Speaking to the media in the White House, Trump said: "We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal.""He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," he continued, seemingly referencing the pair's heated exchange during a meeting in early 2025. "He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer."Zelenskyy and Trump have endured a volatile relationship since the US president began his second term in January last year, but it has soured further in recent weeks after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and criticised the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia's energy sector on global fuel prices.On Tuesday, Trump - who is gearing up for key midterm elections to determine the make-up of Congress for his final two years in office - seemed to pin the blame for the ongoing war on Zelenskyy, repeatedly saying he had had the opportunity to make a deal and that the US had got nothing in return for its help "except grief, death," and "tremendous monetary loss.""We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine; we've got nothing back. Other than high diesel," Trump added. "The American taxpayers are tired of it.""It's time to make a deal," he said.Zelenskyy's Oslo talksTrump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is scheduled to travel to Russia for a meeting with Putin on Wednesday.Following the talks in Oslo, which also involved Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Zelenskyy had appeared relatively positive, telling journalists he had recently held a constructive call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and calling for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin.Zelenskyy also addressed reported restrictions on US intelligence sharing during a press conference with the Nordic leaders, saying he was "thankful" that "intelligence works now.""I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," he said.In a post on social media later in the evening, Zelenskyy added: "It was constructive because all of us want peace – Ukraine, Europe, the United States. And we will see what happens tomorrow."
